claims.evidence: Direct statement describing mosquito trapping methodology.

claims.claim: Mosquito trapping was repeated from June 2015 to July 2015 in communities where no Aedes mosquitoes were found during the initial trapping.
claims.source: To help ensure that communities where no Aedes mosquitoes were found during the initial mosquito trapping truly had no Aedes, mosquito trapping was repeated in these communities from June 2015 to July 2015 during which eight households were randomly selected to have sentinel traps placed in their homes for 24 hr and the traps and mosquitos were processed in the same way as they had been initially.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing additional mosquito surveillance.

claims.claim: The study was approved by the icddr,b ethical review board (protocol number PR-14058).
claims.source: This study was approved by the icddr,b ethical review board (protocol number PR-14058).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of ethical approval.

claims.claim: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention relied on icddr,b's ethical review board approval.
claims.source: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention relied on icddr,b's ethical review board approval.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of ethical approval process.

claims.claim: All adult participants provided written, informed consent after receiving detailed explanation of the study and procedures.
claims.source: All adult participants provided written, informed consent after receiving detailed explanation of the study and procedures.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of consent procedures.

claims.claim: Parents/guardians of all child participants were asked to provide written, informed consent on their behalf.
claims.source: Parents/guardians of all child participants were asked to provide written, informed consent on their behalf.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of consent procedures for children.

claims.claim: Serum was obtained from 76% of household members of participating households.
claims.source: We obtained serum from 76% of household members of participating households (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing participation rate.

claims.claim: Per community there were an average of 95 participants (range 81–116) from 20 households (range 20–23).
claims.source: Per community there were an average of 95 participants (range 81–116) from 20 households (range 20–23).
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing sample characteristics.

claims.claim: The age and sex distributions in the study largely matched those obtained by the 2011 census although there was some under-representation in those <10 years.
claims.source: The age and sex distributions in the study largely matched those obtained by the 2011 census although we had some under-representation in those <10 years (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Direct statement comparing study sample to census data.

claims.claim: The PanBio assay appeared to discriminate well between those with and without past dengue infection.
claims.source: The PanBio assay appeared to discriminate well between those with and without past dengue infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing assay performance.

claims.claim: All communities had at least one seropositive individual.
claims.source: While all communities had at least one seropositive individual, there was substantial spatial heterogeneity across the country with the proportion seropositive ranging from 3% in rural Maulvibazar in Sylhet Division to 88% in urban Chittagong.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing the distribution of seropositivity.

claims.claim: Within Dhaka district, seropositivity ranged from 36 to 85% across three urban communities.
claims.source: Even within Dhaka district (which includes the capital and has the highest population density), where we visited three urban ('Thana') communities, there was substantial heterogeneity, with seropositivity ranging from 36 to 85%.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing heterogeneity within Dhaka.

claims.claim: The two urban communities visited in the city of Chittagong had seropositivities of 84 and 88%.
claims.source: The two urban communities we visited in the city of Chittagong had seropositivities of 84 and 88%.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing seropositivity in Chittagong.

claims.claim: The difference in seropositivity between males and females was concentrated in communities where overall seropositivity was <20%.
claims.source: In particular, males were much more likely to be seropositive (odds ratio [OR]: 1.6 [95%CI: 1.4–1.9]; adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 1.7 [1.5–2.0]), although this difference was concentrated in communities where overall seropositivity was <20% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing stratified analysis.

claims.claim: The estimated number of seropositive individuals in Bangladesh (40.3 million) is much less than the 16.7 million previously estimated through a modelling exercise.
claims.source: Overall, we estimated that around a quarter of the population, around 40 million individuals, have been infected by dengue with an average of 2.4 million annual infections. This figure is much less than the 16.7 million previously estimated through a modelling exercise (Bhatt et al., 2013), highlighting the need for representative data to help support these models and the importance of considering immunity in the estimation of annual case numbers.
claims.evidence: Direct comparison with prior modeling study with citation.

claims.claim: Dengue has only established a pattern of sustained endemic transmission in a few urban settings in Bangladesh, not throughout the country.
claims.source: Our results suggest that since dengue re-emerged in the late 1990 s, the virus has only established a pattern of sustained endemic transmission in a few urban settings, and not throughout the country, as is the case in nearby Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia (Rahman et al., 2002; Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Ministry of health and family Welfare, 2017; van Panhuis et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citations comparing to neighboring countries.

claims.claim: The limited presence of Ae. aegypti may be part of the reason dengue has not established sustained endemic transmission throughout Bangladesh.
claims.source: Part of the reason for this may be the limited presence of the principal vector, Ae. aegypti, which was found in only one third of the communities that participated in this study.
claims.evidence: Direct statement linking vector presence to transmission patterns.

claims.claim: The negative correlation between Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus presence is consistent with the species occupying different environmental niches or competition between the two species.
claims.source: Our finding of a negative correlation between Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus presence is consistent with the species occupying different environmental niches or competition between the two species, as has previously been suggested (Braks et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citation to support interpretation.

claims.claim: All communities had at least one seropositive individual, suggesting that external viral introductions may be common.
claims.source: All communities had at least one seropositive individual, suggesting that external viral introductions may be common and that there may be factors preventing large-scale outbreaks, including from the limited abundance of the Ae. aegypti vector.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference about transmission dynamics.

claims.claim: Comparing infection proportions between males and females can be a good marker of local dengue endemicity.
claims.source: At the individual level, we found that males had 1.6 times the odds of having been infected as females, although this difference was concentrated in communities where overall seropositivity was low, suggesting that comparing infection proportions between males and females can be a good marker of local dengue endemicity.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference from observed patterns.

claims.claim: Individuals from communities with low or no transmission are likely to get infected when they travel to higher transmission areas.
claims.source: These findings suggest that in the current scenario in which infection risk is heterogeneously distributed around the country, individuals from communities with low or no transmission are likely to get infected when they travel to higher transmission areas.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference from travel and seropositivity associations.

claims.claim: If the vector presence expands throughout Bangladesh, individuals who travel could act as sources of outbreaks within their home communities.
claims.source: If the vector presence expands throughout the country, these individuals could act as sources of outbreaks within these communities.
claims.evidence: Direct statement speculating about future transmission dynamics.

claims.claim: The findings for dengue in Bangladesh are in marked contrast to what has been observed with chikungunya, where women were at significantly increased risk of infection.
claims.source: Our findings are in marked contrast to what has been observed with chikungunya in Bangladesh, where women in a community that had a widespread chikungunya epidemic were found to be at significantly increased risk of being infected compared to males, with the increased risk of infection linked to greater time spent in and around the home (Salje et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: Direct comparison with prior study on chikungunya with citation.

claims.claim: It may be difficult to generalize inferences across arboviruses due to differences in vector species and the frequency of introductions and risk of onwards spread.
claims.source: These findings suggest that it may be difficult to generalize inferences across arboviruses due to differences in vector species and the frequency of introductions and risk of onwards spread.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference from comparison of dengue and chikungunya findings.

claims.claim: Incorporating spatial correlation into risk factor regression analyses only resulted in a relatively small improvement in model fit compared to hierarchical models with random intercepts at the community and household levels.
claims.source: While we incorporated spatial correlation into our risk factor regression analyses, in practice this only resulted in a relatively small improvement in model fit compared to hierarchical models with random intercepts at the community and household levels.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing model comparison results.

claims.claim: The biggest impact of incorporating spatial correlation was to move the coefficient estimate for Ae. aegypti presence towards the null.
claims.source: The biggest impact of incorporating the spatial correlation was to move the coefficient estimate for Ae. aegypti presence towards the null.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing the effect of spatial correlation on coefficient estimates.

claims.claim: The spatial covariance structure is a better predictor than basic mosquito absence/presence data because it is driven by and absorbs the true underlying environmental drivers including mosquito distributions.
claims.source: This suggests that the covariance structure is a better predictor than the basic mosquito absence/presence data as the covariance is driven by, and absorbs, the true underlying environmental drivers including mosquito distributions.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference about the role of spatial covariance.

claims.claim: The crude estimate of the proportion seropositive in Bangladesh (24%) was very close to modelled estimates that incorporated age, sex and population distribution (25%).
claims.source: While there was substantial spatial heterogeneity in the risk of being seropositive across the country, ultimately our crude estimates of the proportion seropositive in the country (24%) was very close to modelled estimates that incorporated the age, sex and population distribution in the country (25%).
claims.evidence: Direct comparison of crude and modeled estimates.

claims.claim: The close agreement between crude and modeled estimates provides strong support for the sampling frame used to capture population-level estimates of population exposure.
claims.source: This provides strong support for the sampling frame we used to capture population-level estimates of population exposure.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference about sampling design validity.

claims.claim: Incorporating covariates (e.g., sex, age, population distribution) did not result in substantive improvements in predictive accuracy compared to models that included a spatial covariance term only.
claims.source: Incorporating covariates (e.g., sex, age, population distribution) did not result in substantive improvements in predictive accuracy compared to models that included a spatial covariance term only.
claims.evidence: Direct statement comparing model performance.

claims.claim: The importance of spatial dependence is highlighted for obtaining accurate estimates in unsampled locations.
claims.source: This highlights the importance of spatial dependence in obtaining accurate estimates in unsampled locations.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference from model comparison.

claims.claim: For the Dengvaxia vaccine, the WHO has recommended that countries perform nationally representative serosurveys to inform vaccine rollout.
claims.source: For the only currently licensed vaccine, Dengvaxia, the WHO has recommended that countries perform nationally representative serosurveys to inform vaccine rollout as the vaccine only provides protection in people with existing antibodies (World Health Organization, 2016).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citation to WHO recommendation.

claims.claim: Dengvaxia only provides protection in people with existing antibodies.
claims.source: For the only currently licensed vaccine, Dengvaxia, the WHO has recommended that countries perform nationally representative serosurveys to inform vaccine rollout as the vaccine only provides protection in people with existing antibodies (World Health Organization, 2016).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citation about vaccine characteristics.

claims.claim: The vaccination of seronegative individuals with Dengvaxia has been linked to increased risk of subsequent severe disease.
claims.source: The vaccination of seronegative individuals has been linked to increased risk of subsequent severe disease (Salje et al., 2018; Hadinegoro et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citations to support vaccine safety concern.

claims.claim: Any dengue vaccine rollout in Bangladesh should be concentrated to the urban areas of Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna.
claims.source: For Bangladesh, our findings suggest that any vaccine rollout should be concentrated to the urban areas of Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference from seropositivity findings.

claims.claim: Even in the urban areas of Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna, the proportion seropositive at age 9 years is far below the 80% threshold where vaccine rollout is potentially feasible without pre-vaccination screening.
claims.source: However, even in these communities, the proportion seropositive at age 9 years is far below the threshold of 80% where vaccine rollout is potentially feasible without pre-vaccination screening (World Health Organization, 2018).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citation to WHO threshold.

claims.claim: Any dengue vaccine rollout in Bangladesh will require screening of individuals for presence of antibodies before vaccination.
claims.source: Therefore, any rollout will require the screening of individuals for presence of antibodies before vaccination to avoid placing large numbers of individuals at risk for more severe disease manifestations.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference from seropositivity findings and vaccine characteristics.

claims.claim: Cross-reactivity of antibodies is a problem for all seroprevalence studies, especially with flaviviruses.
claims.source: Cross-reactivity of antibodies is a problem for all seroprevalence studies, especially with flaviviruses.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about methodological limitation.

claims.claim: Cross-reactivity prevents quantifying the relative importance of the different dengue serotypes.
claims.source: This prevents us from quantifying the relative importance of the different dengue serotypes.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about study limitation.

claims.claim: Some seropositive individuals may have been infected with Japanese encephalitis rather than dengue.
claims.source: In addition, some seropositive individuals may have been infected with Japanese encephalitis rather than dengue.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about potential cross-reactivity.

claims.claim: Japanese encephalitis is typically only found in rural communities where it circulates at low levels (estimated at 2.7 cases/100,000).
claims.source: However, Japanese encephalitis is typically only found in rural communities where it circulates at low levels (estimated at 2.7 cases/100,000) (Paul et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citation about Japanese encephalitis epidemiology.

claims.claim: The number of false positives from Japanese encephalitis cross-reactivity is likely to be small because only low levels of dengue seropositivity were estimated in rural communities.
claims.source: As we estimated only low levels of dengue seropositivity in rural communities, the number of false positives from Japanese encephalitis cross-reactivity is likely to be small.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference about the impact of cross-reactivity.

claims.claim: Around 90% of households that were approached agreed to take part in the study.
claims.source: Around 90% of households that we approached agreed to take part in the study.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about participation rate.

claims.claim: BG sentinel traps have been shown to be well suited to trapping Aedes mosquitoes.
claims.source: We used BG sentinel traps that have been shown to be well suited to trapping Aedes mosquitoes (Maciel-de-Freitas et al., 2006; Obenauer et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citations supporting trap choice.

claims.claim: All communities where Aedes mosquitoes were not found in the initial visit were revisited for additional mosquito trapping.
claims.source: In addition, we revisited all communities where we did not find Aedes mosquitoes in the initial visit for additional mosquito trapping.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing additional surveillance effort.

claims.claim: Given the heterogeneous nature of mosquito distributions within communities, Aedes mosquitoes may have been missed in some communities where they breed.
claims.source: However, given the heterogeneous nature of mosquito distributions within communities, we may have nevertheless failed to find Aedes mosquitoes in communities where they breed.
claims.evidence: Direct statement acknowledging potential limitation.

claims.claim: If Aedes mosquitoes were missed in some communities, Aedes may be more widespread than found in this study.
claims.source: This would mean that Aedes may be more widespread than we found.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference about potential underestimation.

claims.claim: Simply asking people about whether or not they had been infected with dengue was not informative of past infection.
claims.source: We found that simply asking people about whether or not they had been infected with dengue was not informative of past infection.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about the limitation of self-reported data.

claims.claim: Studies that only use questionnaires can only provide limited burden information for pathogens such as dengue.
claims.source: This highlights that studies that only use questionnaires can only provide limited burden information for pathogens such as dengue.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference from self-report findings.

claims.claim: Demographic Health Surveys could benefit significantly from adding a serological component to their studies.
claims.source: For example, Demographic Health Surveys, which collect detailed health questionnaires from randomly selected individuals across many countries could benefit significantly from adding a serological component to their studies.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference about improving survey methods.

claims.claim: In Bangladesh, where dengue is still emerging, surveillance for vectors could be a way to monitor risk of future outbreaks.
claims.source: In Bangladesh, where dengue is still emerging, surveillance for vectors could be a way to monitor risk of future outbreaks and continued efforts to understand drivers of transmission could point to interventions to reduce its geographic spread.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference about surveillance strategies.

claims.claim: Nationally representative serum banks are a powerful tool for public health agencies to understand pathogen circulation patterns, vaccination levels, and the existence of spatial pockets of susceptibility.
claims.source: By tracking the levels of pathogen-specific antibodies in populations, these banks are a powerful tool for public health agencies to understand a wide range of factors that can assist in the fight against diseases, including pathogen circulation patterns, vaccination levels, and the existence of spatial pockets of susceptibility (De Melker and Conyn-van Spaendonck, 1998; Gidding et al., 2005; Osborne et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citations supporting the utility of serum banks.

claims.claim: To date, the accumulation and use of nationally representative banked sera have focused almost exclusively on vaccine preventable childhood infections.
claims.source: To date, the accumulation and use of nationally representative banked sera have focused almost exclusively on vaccine preventable childhood infections.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about historical focus of serum banks.

claims.claim: Serum banks have the potential to be invaluable in efforts to understand the burden from arboviruses and optimize efforts for control, including the targeted deployment of vaccines.
claims.source: However, serum banks also have the potential to be invaluable in efforts to understand the burden from arboviruses and optimize efforts for control, including the targeted deployment of vaccines (Imai and Ferguson, 2018).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citation about potential applications.

claims.claim: High levels of subclinical infection and frequent clinical misclassification mean that even in locations with good disease surveillance, the underlying risk of dengue infection is poorly understood.
claims.source: In these diseases, high levels of subclinical infection and frequent clinical misclassification mean that even in locations with good disease surveillance, the underlying risk of infection is poorly understood (Halstead, 2007).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citation about challenges in dengue surveillance.

claims.claim: Studies that collect serum for the detection of pathogen-specific antibodies typically rely on either convenience samples or focus on single communities, often in major cities or where the perceived risk of the pathogen is believed to be greatest.
claims.source: Studies that collect serum for the detection of pathogen-specific antibodies typically rely on either convenience samples (e.g., blood donations) or focus on single communities, often in major cities or where the perceived risk of the pathogen is believed to be greatest (Petersen et al., 2012; Salje et al., 2016a; Rodríguez-Barraquer et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citations about typical serostudy designs.

claims.claim: The ability to generalize results from convenience samples or single-community studies to the wider population is rarely known.
claims.source: While they are often a good starting place for understanding historic pathogen circulation in the sampled communities and age-groups, the ability to generalize the results to the wider population is rarely known.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about limitations of typical serostudy designs.

claims.claim: If communities are randomly chosen from across a country, we can estimate national incidence rates, the underlying spatial heterogeneity in burden, the spatial dependence across neighbouring communities and identify risk factors for infection.
claims.source: By contrast, if communities are randomly chosen from across a country, we can estimate national incidence rates, the underlying spatial heterogeneity in burden, the spatial dependence across neighbouring communities and identify risk factors for infection.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about advantages of nationally representative sampling.

claims.claim: Nationally representative study designs provide mechanistic insights into pathogen spread and facilitate the development of data-informed control policies.
claims.source: Such study designs therefore provide mechanistic insights into pathogen spread and facilitate the development of data-informed control policies.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about benefits of nationally representative designs.

claims.claim: Transmission of arboviruses, such as dengue, appears to be driven by the interplay of individual-, household-, and community-level factors.
claims.source: Transmission of arboviruses, such as dengue, appears to be driven by the interplay of individual- (e.g., sex, age, travel), household- (e.g., water supply, use of mosquito control) and community-level (e.g., urban/rural, mosquito abundance) factors (Salje et al., 2016b; Rodríguez-Barraquer et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citations about transmission dynamics.

claims.claim: To make data-informed decisions on how best to control dengue spread, we need to understand the relative importance of different factors by collecting detailed data across individual, household, and community scales.
claims.source: In order to make data-informed decisions on how best to control spread, we need to understand the relative importance of these different factors by collecting detailed data across these scales.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about data needs for control strategies.

claims.claim: A recent literature search found only one nationally representative dengue seroprevalence study, from Singapore, but there was only a subset of age-groups considered.
claims.source: A recent literature search found only one nationally representative dengue seroprevalence study, from Singapore, but there was only a subset of age-groups considered (Imai et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with citation about prior nationally representative studies.

claims.claim: In rural locations in Bangladesh (around three-quarters of the country), census-communities consist of villages, whereas in urban places, these communities are city wards.
claims.source: In rural locations (around three-quarters of the country), these census-communities consist of villages, whereas in urban places, these communities are city wards.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing community definitions.

claims.claim: The study team spent at least 5 days in each community during each visit.
claims.source: For each visit, the study team spent at least 5 days in the community.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing field procedures.

claims.claim: Data collection for a community was considered complete when at least 40 serum samples from at least 10 households had been collected.
claims.source: Data collection for a community was considered to be complete when at least 40 serum samples from at least 10 households had been collected.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing sampling targets.

claims.claim: Residents were offered a test to determine their blood group as a benefit of participating.
claims.source: Residents were offered a test to determine their blood group as a benefit of participating.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing participant incentive.

claims.claim: A phlebotomist collected 5 ml of venous blood from all individuals who gave consent.
claims.source: A phlebotomist collected 5 ml of venous blood from all individuals who gave consent.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing sample collection procedure.

claims.claim: Individuals who were sick at the time of blood collection were ineligible.
claims.source: Individuals who were sick at the time were ineligible.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing exclusion criteria.

claims.claim: Blood samples were centrifuged in the field and the serum extracted into separate vials before being shipped to icddr,b laboratories in Dhaka in nitrogen dry shippers.
claims.source: These samples were centrifuged in the field and the serum extracted into separate vials before being shipped to icddr,b (previously known as the international centre for diarrhoeal disease research, Bangladesh) laboratories in Dhaka in nitrogen dry shippers.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing sample processing and transport.

claims.claim: The study used hierarchical models with random intercepts for household and community to account for clustering.
claims.source: For each covariate, we initially performed simple logistic regression to explore associations with dengue serostatus using a hierarchical model with random intercepts for household and community.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing statistical methods.

claims.claim: The study accounted for spatial correlation structure using a Matern covariance function using a stochastic partial differential equation.
claims.source: We accounted for spatial correlation structure using a Matern covariance function using a stochastic partial differential equation and fitted the models using integrated nested Laplace approximations (INLA) in a Bayesian framework (Lindgren et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing statistical methods with citation.

claims.claim: Models were fitted using integrated nested Laplace approximations (INLA) in a Bayesian framework.
claims.source: We accounted for spatial correlation structure using a Matern covariance function using a stochastic partial differential equation and fitted the models using integrated nested Laplace approximations (INLA) in a Bayesian framework (Lindgren et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing statistical methods with citation.

claims.claim: A sensitivity model was performed using only individuals > 20 years to assess whether results were affected by age-related differences in past dengue circulation.
claims.source: As the probability of being seropositive is strongly linked to the past circulation of dengue, we also performed a sensitivity model in which we recalculated the regressions using only individuals > 20 years as seropositivity was not found to differ by age among older adults.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing sensitivity analysis.

claims.claim: A 5 km x 5 km grid was placed over Bangladesh to estimate the population size in each grid cell using data from worldpop.org.
claims.source: To explore the variability in dengue risk across Bangladesh, we initially placed a 5 km x 5 km grid over the country and estimated the population size in each of those grid cells using data available from worldpop.org (Tatem, 2017).
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing spatial prediction methodology with citation.

claims.claim: The fitted spatial prediction model was used to predict in unsampled grid cells by drawing 1000 samples from the posterior for each grid cell.
claims.source: We used the fitted model to predict in the unsampled grid cells by drawing 1000 samples from the posterior for each grid cell and calculated the mean as well as 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles to quantify uncertainty.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing prediction methodology.

claims.claim: The estimated number of seropositive individuals in a grid cell was calculated by multiplying the estimated proportion seropositive in a cell by the population within that cell.
claims.source: The estimated number of seropositive individuals in a cell was calculated by multiplying the estimated proportion seropositive in a cell by the population within that cell.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing calculation method.

claims.claim: The total number of seropositive individuals in Bangladesh was calculated as the sum of seropositive individuals across all the grid cells.
claims.source: The total number of seropositive individuals in the country was calculated as the sum of seropositive individuals across all the grid cells.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing calculation method.

claims.claim: A sensitivity analysis predicted the spatial distribution of dengue seropositivity using a model with the Matern spatial covariance matrix only (without any covariates).
claims.source: As a sensitivity analysis, we also predicted the spatial distribution of dengue seropositivity in the country using a model with the Matern spatial covariance matrix only (i.e., without any covariates).
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing sensitivity analysis.

claims.claim: Four different models were assessed for their ability to accurately predict the level of seropositivity in unsampled locations: crude proportion seropositive, multivariable logistic model with spatial covariance, multivariable logistic model without spatial dependence, and spatial dependence model with no covariates.
claims.source: We considered four different models: (i) crude proportion seropositive, (ii) multivariable logistic model with sex, age-group and population size as covariates and Matern spatial covariance (the baseline model), (iii) multivariable logistic model with sex, age-group and population size as covariates but with no spatial dependence, and (iv) spatial dependence model using Matern spatial covariance with no covariates.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing model comparison approach.

claims.claim: For model validation, subsets of communities were repeatedly randomly selected to train the model (varied between 2, 20, 40, 60 and 69 communities) and seroprevalence was predicted in the remaining communities.
claims.source: For 100 iterations and for each model in turn, we repeatedly randomly selected a subset of communities to train the model (varied between 2, 20, 40, 60 and 69 communities) and predicted the seroprevalence in the remaining communities not used to fit the model.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing validation methodology.

claims.claim: The study assessed the impact of sampling fewer people per community by rerunning models with between 2 and 80 individuals sampled per community.
claims.source: Separately, we considered the impact of having sampled fewer people per community. We reran each of the four models over repeated iterations using 50 randomly selected communities and with between 2 and 80 individuals sampled per community to train the models.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing sensitivity analysis on sample size.

claims.claim: Catalytic models were used to estimate the proportion of the susceptible population that get infected each year using the probability of being seropositive as a function of age.
claims.source: We used the probability of being seropositive as a function of age to estimate the proportion of the susceptible population that get infected each year using catalytic models, an approach which has been used frequently to reconstruct the past circulation of pathogens (Salje et al., 2016a; Rodríguez-Barraquer et al., 2014; Imai et al., 2015; Ferguson et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing analytical approach with citations.

claims.claim: The catalytic model assumed a constant force of infection due to all four serotypes and that there were no differences in risk by age.
claims.source: We assumed a constant force of infection due to all four serotypes, λ and that there were no differences in risk by age.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing model assumptions.

claims.claim: The number of years prior to 2014 that dengue has circulated in Bangladesh (NYears) was fixed at 20 years.
claims.source: We fixed NYears at 20 to reflect the approximate period when dengue first appeared in the country.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing model parameter.

claims.claim: A sensitivity analysis varied the number of years dengue has circulated (NYears) between 15 and 25 years.
claims.source: We conducted a sensitivity analysis where this was varied between 15 and 25 years.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing sensitivity analysis.

claims.claim: The force of infection was calculated separately by sex and for the three largest cities versus the rest of the country.
claims.source: We calculated the force of infection for the entire sampled population as well as separate estimates by sex and for the locations from the three largest cities (Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna) only versus the rest of the country.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing stratified analyses.

claims.claim: To estimate the number of people infected each year, the study used the estimated population by age for each year for the period 1995–2014.
claims.source: To estimate the number of people infected each year we used the estimated population by age for each year for the period 1995–2014 (Kinsella and He, 2009).
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing data source with citation.

claims.claim: The model assumed that in 1995, the entire population was susceptible to dengue.
claims.source: We assumed that in 1995, the entire population was susceptible.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing model assumption.

claims.claim: The serotype specific force of infection was calculated as λ/4.
claims.source: The proportion of the population that have monotypic immunity is calculated as w(a,y)=4 x exp(−3 x λs x a*) x (1-exp(-λs x a*)) where λs is the serotype specific force of infection and is calculated as λ/4
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing calculation method.

claims.claim: The study estimated the number of primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary dengue infections.
claims.source: Using these proportions we can calculate the number of primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary dengue infections.
claims.evidence: Direct statement describing model outputs.

claims.claim: The estimated total number of infections presented includes primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary infections.
claims.source: We present the estimated total number of infections across primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary infections.

claims.claim: There has been growing recognition of the utility of nationally representative serum banks to monitor the burden from infectious diseases in a population.
claims.source: There has been growing recognition of the utility of nationally representative serum banks to monitor the burden from infectious diseases in a population (Metcalf et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2012; Osborne et al., 1997; Jardine et al., 2010; De Melker and Conyn-van Spaendonck, 1998; van der Klis et al., 2009).

claims.source: However, in cultural contexts where marriage rates may vary by community or location within a community, this method of choosing a random starting point could produce a biased sample.

claims.claim: Given that >95% of adults marry in Bangladesh, it is unlikely that the approach of using recent weddings to identify a starting point could bias the sample obtained.
claims.source: Therefore, we used a quasi-random approach that identified a starting point for household sampling based on the area of the community where the most recent wedding took place; given that >95% of adults marry in Bangladesh, it is unlikely that this approach could bias the sample we obtained.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with inference about sampling method validity in Bangladesh context.

results.result: A nationally representative serosurvey was conducted in Bangladesh using probability-proportional-to-size sampling of 70 communities from 97,162 census communities, with two visits during 2014-2016, achieving 5,866 participants (76% of household members) with age/sex distributions largely matching the 2011 census.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C57-C59, and C93 collectively demonstrate rigorous sampling methodology with clear documentation of selection procedures, participation rates, and representativeness. The probability-proportional-to-size sampling from a complete census frame, high participation rate (76% of household members, 90% of households), and demographic matching to census data provide strong evidence for the representativeness of the sample.

results.result: Overall dengue seroprevalence in Bangladesh was 24%, with substantial spatial heterogeneity ranging from 3% in rural Sylhet to 88% in urban Chittagong, and demographic variation showing 27% in males vs 21% in females (p<0.001) and 30% in those >20 years vs 14% in those <20 years.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C11-C12, and C61-C63 provide consistent descriptive statistics with appropriate statistical testing (p-values reported). The spatial heterogeneity is well-documented across multiple geographic scales (national, divisional, and city-level), and demographic patterns are clearly quantified with statistical significance testing.

results.result: Male sex (aOR: 1.7 [1.5-2.0]) and recent travel within 7 days (aOR: 1.4 [1.1-1.8]) were significant risk factors for dengue seropositivity, with the sex difference concentrated in low-seroprevalence communities (<20%), suggesting male-female seropositivity ratios may serve as markers of local endemicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14, C64, and C70 present regression results with both unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios with confidence intervals. The stratified analysis by community seroprevalence level (C64) strengthens the interpretation. However, the mechanistic explanation for why sex differences concentrate in low-prevalence areas remains inferential.

results.result: Household-level factors including electricity, water access, land ownership, household income, and mosquito control use were not associated with dengue seropositivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 clearly report null findings with confidence intervals crossing 1.0 for odds ratios. These negative results are important for understanding transmission dynamics, though the lack of association could reflect measurement issues, insufficient statistical power for household-level effects, or genuine absence of effects.

results.result: Ae. aegypti presence showed some association with seropositivity (OR 1.8 [1.2-2.8], aOR 1.4 [0.9-2.2]), while Ae. albopictus presence showed no association (aOR 1.0 [0.7-1.6]). The two species showed slight negative correlation (r=-0.2, p=0.07), and incorporating spatial correlation reduced the Ae. aegypti coefficient toward the null.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C23, C76-C77 present mosquito surveillance data and associations, but the adjusted confidence interval for Ae. aegypti crosses 1.0 (0.9-2.2), indicating statistical uncertainty. The authors acknowledge that spatial covariance may be a better predictor than mosquito presence/absence data (C77), suggesting the mosquito surveillance may have been insufficiently sensitive or that spatial correlation captures unmeasured environmental drivers.

results.result: Population size (log scale) was associated with increased seropositivity (OR 1.3 [1.2-1.5]). Variance partitioning showed spatial covariance explained 15%, community random effects 6%, and household random effects 12% of variance, with spatial correlation providing modest improvement in model fit (DIC difference of 4).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 and C75 provide clear statistical evidence for urbanization effects and variance partitioning. The DIC comparison justifies inclusion of spatial correlation, though the improvement is modest. The variance partitioning provides important insights into the hierarchical structure of transmission.

results.result: Approximately 25% (95% CI: 21-29%) of Bangladesh's population, equivalent to 40.3 million individuals (95% CI: 34.3-47.2), had been infected with dengue, with crude estimates (24%) closely matching modeled estimates (25%), validating the sampling framework.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30, C78-C79 present national burden estimates with appropriate uncertainty quantification. The close agreement between crude and modeled estimates (24% vs 25%) provides internal validation of the sampling design and modeling approach. However, these estimates assume the serological assay correctly identifies dengue exposure without cross-reactivity issues.

results.result: Spatial correlation in seropositivity extended to 108 km, and spatial prediction models performed well (Pearson r=0.8, MAE=8%) without requiring demographic covariates, highlighting the importance of spatial dependence for predictions in unsampled locations.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32, C80-C81 demonstrate strong model performance with appropriate validation metrics. The finding that spatial correlation alone performs as well as models with covariates is important for understanding transmission patterns and has practical implications for survey design.

results.result: Catalytic modeling estimated 1.6% (95% CI: 1.5-1.7%) annual infection rate nationally, equivalent to 2.4 million infections/year (95% CI: 2.2-2.5), with substantial geographic variation: 6.4% (5.4-7.6%) annually in major urban hubs (Dhaka, Chittagong, Khulna) versus 1.0% (0.9-1.2%) for females and 1.6% (1.4-1.8%) for males elsewhere.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 present force of infection estimates from catalytic models, but these rely on strong assumptions including constant force of infection across time (C133), 20 years of circulation (C134), and equal risk across ages (C133). The model assumes all seropositive individuals were infected in Bangladesh, potentially overestimating local transmission if some infections were acquired through travel. Sensitivity analyses on time period (C135) are mentioned but results not fully presented.

results.result: Sensitivity analyses showed that sampling 20 communities would yield highly variable seroprevalence estimates (13-37%), while 60 communities provided more stable estimates (22-28%). Spatial model performance improved substantially with more communities (MAE: 13.6% with 20 communities to 10.5% with 69; correlation: 0.39 to 0.81), while sampling 20 vs 80 individuals per community had minimal impact.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 provide rigorous sensitivity analyses demonstrating the importance of sampling many communities rather than many individuals per community. The iterative resampling approach (100 iterations, C130) provides robust estimates of sampling variability. These findings have important implications for future survey design.

results.result: Seropositivity was highly correlated between 2014 and 2015 visits (Pearson r=0.92) with no significant difference in overall seropositivity across years (p=0.66).
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 demonstrate temporal stability in community-level seroprevalence. However, the authors acknowledge (in discussion) that the study was not powered to detect small changes and that sampling different households in each year limited ability to measure incidence. The high correlation primarily reflects spatial heterogeneity rather than temporal dynamics.

results.result: Despite 91% awareness of dengue among those >10 years, only 0.6% (38/5866) reported prior dengue infection, and only 16 of these 38 were seropositive, demonstrating that self-reported infection history is uninformative for dengue burden estimation.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C98-C99 clearly demonstrate the disconnect between awareness, self-reported infection, and serological evidence. This finding is important for understanding limitations of questionnaire-based surveillance and supports the need for serological surveys.

results.result: The estimated 40.3 million seropositive individuals in Bangladesh is substantially lower than the 16.7 million previously estimated by Bhatt et al. (2013) modeling exercise.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 compares cumulative infections (40.3 million ever infected) with annual infections from a prior model (16.7 million), which may not be directly comparable. The claim states the current estimate is "much less" but the comparison appears to conflate cumulative prevalence with annual incidence. The citation to Bhatt et al. 2013 should be verified to confirm what was actually estimated in that study.

results.result: Dengue has established sustained endemic transmission only in a few urban settings in Bangladesh, not throughout the country as in neighboring Myanmar, Thailand, and Cambodia. Limited Ae. aegypti presence (33% of communities) may explain this pattern, with negative correlation between Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus suggesting niche partitioning or competition.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 synthesize multiple lines of evidence (spatial heterogeneity, vector distributions, universal presence of at least one seropositive individual) to infer transmission patterns. The interpretation is reasonable given the data, though the comparison to neighboring countries relies on cited literature rather than direct comparison. The inference about vector limitation is plausible but not definitively proven.

results.result: Individuals from low-transmission communities likely acquire infections when traveling to high-transmission areas, and could serve as sources of outbreaks in their home communities if vector presence expands.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 present reasonable inferences from the travel and seropositivity associations, but C72 is explicitly speculative ("If the vector presence expands..."). The travel data (time since last leaving community) is crude and doesn't capture destination or duration. The causal pathway from travel to infection to local transmission requires assumptions about viremia timing and vector competence.

results.result: The male-biased dengue seropositivity contrasts with female-biased chikungunya infection risk in Bangladesh, suggesting difficulty in generalizing risk factors across arboviruses due to differences in vector species and transmission dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 make an appropriate comparison to prior work (Salje et al. 2016b) and draw a reasonable inference about arbovirus-specific transmission patterns. The contrast between dengue and chikungunya sex patterns is well-documented and the interpretation about vector and transmission differences is plausible.

results.result: WHO recommends nationally representative serosurveys for Dengvaxia vaccine deployment because the vaccine only protects seropositive individuals and increases severe disease risk in seronegative individuals. For Bangladesh, vaccine rollout should target urban Dhaka, Chittagong, and Khulna, but even there, seropositivity at age 9 is below the 80% threshold for vaccination without pre-screening, necessitating individual antibody screening before vaccination.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87 appropriately cite WHO guidance and vaccine characteristics, and logically apply the study findings to vaccine policy. The recommendation for pre-vaccination screening is well-justified given the seropositivity data. However, the age 9 threshold and 80% cutoff come from WHO guidance (C86) rather than being derived in this study.

results.result: Cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses, particularly Japanese encephalitis, is a limitation that prevents serotype-specific quantification and may cause false positives, though the impact is likely small because Japanese encephalitis circulates at low levels (2.7 cases/100,000) primarily in rural areas where dengue seropositivity was low.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 appropriately acknowledge a key limitation of serological studies and provide a reasonable assessment of its likely impact. The logic that false positives from JE would be minimal in rural areas where dengue seropositivity was already low is sound. However, no direct testing for JE antibodies was performed to quantify this potential bias.

results.result: BG sentinel traps were used for mosquito surveillance with repeat visits to communities where Aedes were not initially found, but the heterogeneous nature of mosquito distributions means Aedes may have been missed in some communities, potentially underestimating vector distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 appropriately describe the mosquito surveillance methods with citations supporting trap choice, acknowledge the repeat sampling effort, and honestly discuss limitations. The acknowledgment of potential underestimation due to spatial heterogeneity is appropriate given that only 8 households per community were sampled.

results.result: Nationally representative serum banks are powerful tools for understanding pathogen circulation, vaccination levels, and susceptibility pockets, but have historically focused on vaccine-preventable childhood infections. Adding serological components to surveys like Demographic Health Surveys could improve arbovirus burden estimation, and vector surveillance could help monitor outbreak risk in Bangladesh.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C104 present reasonable recommendations based on the study findings and cited literature. The suggestions for enhancing existing survey platforms and implementing vector surveillance are logical extensions of the work, though they represent future directions rather than findings from this study.

results.result: Optimal community sampling density depends on population distribution, infection heterogeneity, precision requirements, and budget, but the 108 km spatial correlation suggests sampling at least one community per 100 km radius. Sampling 20 individuals per community provides robust estimates with fewer budget constraints than visiting additional communities.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C145 provide practical guidance for future survey design based on the spatial correlation findings (C31) and sensitivity analyses (C38-C42). The recommendations are well-justified by the data, though the specific 100 km threshold is somewhat arbitrary given the continuous nature of spatial correlation.

results.result: Serum samples were tested using PanBio indirect IgG ELISAs, which appeared to discriminate well between those with and without past dengue infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C60 describe the serological assay used, but C60's assessment that the assay "appeared to discriminate well" is based only on visual inspection of a figure (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) without quantitative validation metrics. No sensitivity/specificity data, comparison to neutralization assays, or assessment of cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses is provided beyond the general discussion of cross-reactivity limitations.

results.result: The quasi-random household sampling approach using recent wedding locations as starting points is unlikely to bias the sample in Bangladesh where >95% of adults marry, though this approach could produce bias in contexts where marriage rates vary spatially. More detailed movement tracking (GPS, diaries) would improve understanding of mobility patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C148 appropriately discuss limitations and context-specificity of the sampling approach. The justification for the wedding-based starting point is reasonable for Bangladesh but the authors appropriately note it may not generalize. The suggestion for improved movement tracking is a reasonable recommendation for future work.

results.result: The study received ethical approval from icddr,b (protocol PR-14058), with CDC relying on this approval, and obtained written informed consent from all adult participants and parents/guardians of children.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 document appropriate ethical procedures. These are standard reporting requirements and appear to have been properly followed.

results.result: Statistical analyses used hierarchical models with random intercepts for household and community, incorporated spatial correlation via Matern covariance functions fitted with INLA in a Bayesian framework, and included sensitivity analyses restricted to adults >20 years.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C123 describe appropriate and sophisticated statistical methods with proper citations (Lindgren et al. 2011). The hierarchical structure accounts for clustering, spatial correlation addresses geographic dependence, and sensitivity analyses address potential confounding by age-related exposure history. The methods are well-suited to the data structure.

results.result: Catalytic models estimated force of infection from age-seroprevalence relationships, assuming constant force of infection across four serotypes with no age-related risk differences, 20 years of circulation (sensitivity: 15-25 years), and complete susceptibility in 1995. Models estimated primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary infections separately by sex and for major cities versus rest of country.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C141 describe the catalytic modeling approach with appropriate citations, but the assumptions are quite strong and may not hold. Constant force of infection (C133) is unlikely given the documented spatial heterogeneity and temporal variation in dengue transmission. The assumption of complete susceptibility in 1995 (C138) ignores potential earlier circulation. The 20-year circulation period (C134) is described as "approximate" without clear justification. While sensitivity analyses on the time period were conducted (C135), results are not fully presented. These assumptions substantially affect the infection rate estimates.
